blocks.content: Say your friend runs a food delivery app and tells you "our system is reliable." That sentence means nothing on its own. Reliable compared to what? Measured how? Reliable enough for who?

SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs are the three terms that turn "reliable" into something you can actually measure, target, and promise. They get used interchangeably by people who have not sat down and separated them, and that confusion causes real problems, like a team chasing an internal number that has nothing to do with what they promised a customer.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396352642-206439502.png
blocks.alt: The SLI feeds the SLO, which sits stricter than the external SLA

blocks.content: This lesson untangles all three, then builds the practical tool teams actually use day to day: the error budget.
1. SLI: the raw measured number
An SLI, Service Level Indicator, is just a measurement. Nothing more. It is a number you compute from real traffic hitting your real system, right now, today.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396357425-268108762.png
blocks.alt: Requests hit the service and get measured into a single SLI number

blocks.content: ["Percentage of requests that returned a successful status code","p99 latency of your API over the last hour","Percentage of background jobs that completed before their deadline","Percentage of pages that finished loading under two seconds"]
items: Percentage of requests that returned a successful status code
p99 latency of your API over the last hour
Percentage of background jobs that completed before their deadline
Percentage of pages that finished loading under two seconds

blocks.content: Notice none of these say what is "good enough." An SLI has no opinion about whether 99.87 percent success is fine or a disaster. It is just what happened. The opinion comes next, with the SLO.

blocks.title: SLIs need a clear formula
blocks.content: Before you can target or promise anything, everyone on the team needs to agree on exactly how the SLI is computed, over what time window, counting which requests. "Success rate" is ambiguous until you define whether timeouts count as failures and whether health checks count as requests at all.
2. SLO: the internal target
An SLO, Service Level Objective, is the target your team sets for an SLI. It is the answer to "how good does this number need to be for us to consider the system healthy?"
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396357427-260373797.png
blocks.alt: The team looks at the measured SLI and sets an internal target on top of it, the SLO

blocks.content: A typical SLO reads like this: 99.9 percent of requests succeed, measured over a rolling 30 day window. That single sentence names the SLI being tracked, the bar it needs to clear, and the time period the bar applies to.
{"headers":["Part of the SLO","Example value"],"rows":[["SLI being tracked","Percentage of successful requests"],["Target","99.9 percent"],["Window","Rolling 30 days"]]}

SLOs are internal. Nobody outside the engineering org needs to see this number, and it can be as strict or specific as the team finds useful. Some teams track five or six SLOs at once, one for availability, one for latency, one for a specific critical endpoint.

blocks.title: An SLO without a time window is not really an SLO
blocks.content: Ninety nine point nine percent measured over one minute is a totally different promise than the same number measured over thirty days. Always pin down the window, or the target is meaningless.
3. SLA: the external promise
An SLA, Service Level Agreement, is a contract. It is what you promise a paying customer, usually in writing, usually with real consequences attached if you miss it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396357428-295952203.png
blocks.alt: The provider signs a contractual SLA promise to the customer, backed by credits if missed

blocks.content: A cloud provider might promise 99.95 percent uptime per month. Miss it, and customers get a service credit on their next bill, a percentage refund, sometimes an outright contractual penalty. This is the piece with legal and financial weight behind it.

["SLA target is usually looser than the internal SLO for the same metric","SLA breach has real consequences: credits, refunds, penalty clauses","SLA is external facing, written for customers and sales, not engineers","SLA measurement rules are often spelled out precisely in a contract, including what counts as an outage"]
items: SLA target is usually looser than the internal SLO for the same metric
SLA breach has real consequences: credits, refunds, penalty clauses
SLA is external facing, written for customers and sales, not engineers
SLA measurement rules are often spelled out precisely in a contract, including what counts as an outage

blocks.content: An SLA is a promise with money attached. An SLO is a promise you make to yourself so you never have to test whether the SLA promise holds.
4. Why the SLO should be stricter than the SLA
blocks.text: 4. Why the SLO should be stricter than the SLA

blocks.content: This is the part that trips people up on their first read. Why bother having two different numbers for basically the same thing? Because you want to find out about degradation from your own dashboards, not from an angry customer citing the contract.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396357428-826111061.png
blocks.alt: A buffer zone sits between the stricter internal SLO and the looser external SLA

blocks.content: If your SLA promises 99.5 percent and your internal SLO is also 99.5 percent, the first time something goes even slightly wrong, you have already broken the contract. There is zero room to notice, react, and fix things before it becomes a customer facing, invoice affecting event.
Setting the SLO at 99.9 percent, tighter than the 99.5 percent SLA, gives you a buffer. You start getting internal signals and pages well before you are anywhere near breaching the actual contract.

{"headers":["Signal","Meaning"],"rows":[["SLO violated, SLA still fine","Early warning. Fix it now, customers never notice."],["SLA violated","Too late. Contract is broken, credits owed, trust damaged."]]}

blocks.title: The gap is the whole point
blocks.content: If your SLO and SLA are set to the same number, you have built a system with no early warning at all. The gap between them is not slack you forgot to tighten, it is intentional runway.
5. Error budgets: the practical tool built on an SLO
blocks.text: 5. Error budgets: the practical tool built on an SLO

blocks.content: Once you have an SLO, you automatically have something else for free: an error budget. If your SLO is 99.9 percent success, then 0.1 percent of requests are allowed to fail and you are still meeting your own target.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396357429-664001249.png
blocks.alt: The SLO target leaves a remaining slice, the error budget, available to spend

blocks.content: That 0.1 percent is not waste or an admission of failure. It is a budget, a concrete, spendable amount of allowed unreliability that the team gets to use deliberately.
5.1 What you can spend the budget on
blocks.text: 5.1 What you can spend the budget on

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396357430-919227430.png
blocks.alt: The available error budget gets spent on a risky deploy or planned maintenance

blocks.content: ["Shipping a riskier deploy without waiting for extra safety nets","Taking planned downtime for a maintenance window or migration","Rolling out a new feature to production faster than usual","Accepting a known, temporary degradation while fixing something bigger"]
items: Shipping a riskier deploy without waiting for extra safety nets
Taking planned downtime for a maintenance window or migration
Rolling out a new feature to production faster than usual
Accepting a known, temporary degradation while fixing something bigger

blocks.content: If the budget is nearly gone, the answer flips. The team slows down, freezes risky deploys, and spends the next stretch of time purely on reliability work until the budget refills.

blocks.title: A full error budget is a green light, not a badge of shame
blocks.content: Teams sometimes treat every single failed request as a bug to chase immediately. An error budget reframes that: as long as you are within budget, some failures are simply the cost of moving fast, and that is fine by design.
6. Error budget burn rate and alerting
blocks.text: 6. Error budget burn rate and alerting

blocks.content: Knowing you have an error budget is not enough by itself, you also need to know how fast you are spending it. That is the burn rate: the speed at which failures are eating into the remaining budget.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396357430-441401386.png
blocks.alt: A fast burn rate on the error budget triggers an alert to the on call team

blocks.content: A budget of 0.1 percent over 30 days can absorb a small trickle of failures spread evenly across the month without anyone noticing. But if you burn through the entire 30 day budget in one hour, that is a five alarm fire, even though the raw failure percentage in that hour might look similar to a bad but survivable day.
6.1 Burn rate versus a single static threshold
blocks.text: 6.1 Burn rate versus a single static threshold

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396357431-431254978.png
blocks.alt: A static threshold reacts late while burn rate alerting catches the trend early

blocks.content: A static threshold alert, like "page if error rate exceeds 1 percent right now," reacts to a single bad snapshot and can both miss slow leaks and cry wolf on brief blips. Burn rate alerting instead asks "at this rate, when would we exhaust the whole budget," and pages differently depending on the answer: minutes away is an emergency, weeks away is a ticket for later.

{"headers":["Burn rate","Time to exhaust 30 day budget","Response"],"rows":[["1x, the expected rate","30 days","Normal, no action"],["10x","About 3 days","Urgent, investigate today"],["60x","About 12 hours","Page immediately, treat as an incident"]]}

This ties directly into the dedicated alerting topic in this module: burn rate is simply one of the smartest signals you can alert on, because it accounts for both how bad things are and how fast they are getting worse.
7. Choosing good SLOs

An SLO is only useful if it reflects something users actually feel. It is tempting to pick an SLO because it is easy to measure, CPU usage, memory, some internal queue depth, rather than because it reflects real user pain.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396357431-496834800.png
blocks.alt: A metric gets checked against whether it reflects real user pain before becoming an SLO

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Reflects user experience"],"rows":[["Checkout request success rate","Yes, directly tied to whether users can buy something"],["p99 latency on the search endpoint","Yes, users feel slow search"],["Average CPU utilization","No, users never see CPU, only the outcomes it affects"],["Number of log lines written per second","No, purely internal, meaningless to a user"]]}

A good rule of thumb: if you cannot explain in one sentence how a real user would notice this metric moving, it probably should not be an SLO. Track it if you want for debugging, but do not build your reliability targets or your alerting around it.

blocks.title: Fewer, sharper SLOs beat many vague ones
blocks.content: Teams that pick two or three SLOs tied tightly to core user journeys, like checkout or login, tend to get more value than teams tracking twenty metrics loosely because they were all easy to instrument.
8. Worked example: from traffic to an error budget
blocks.text: 8. Worked example: from traffic to an error budget

blocks.content: Let us make this concrete with real numbers. Say you run an API service with an SLO of 99.9 percent successful requests over a rolling 30 day window, and the service handles 30 million requests over that month.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396357432-932983160.png
blocks.alt: 30 million requests and a 0.1 percent error budget produce 30000 allowed failures

blocks.content:
total_requests = 30_000_000
slo_target = 0.999          # 99.9 percent

error_budget_fraction = 1 - slo_target      # 0.001, i.e. 0.1 percent
allowed_failures = total_requests * error_budget_fraction

print(allowed_failures)     # 30000.0

code.content:
total_requests = 30_000_000
slo_target = 0.999          # 99.9 percent

error_budget_fraction = 1 - slo_target      # 0.001, i.e. 0.1 percent
allowed_failures = total_requests * error_budget_fraction

print(allowed_failures)     # 30000.0

codes.python:
def main():
    total_requests = 30_000_000
    slo_target = 0.999          # 99.9 percent

    error_budget_fraction = 1 - slo_target      # 0.001, i.e. 0.1 percent
    allowed_failures = total_requests * error_budget_fraction

    print(allowed_failures)     # 30000.0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: So this team is allowed 30000 failed requests across the whole month while still meeting its own internal SLO. That is a real, spendable number an on call engineer can reason about: "we have burned 12000 of our 30000 allowed failures so far this month, we still have room."
8.1 Layering the customer facing SLA on top
blocks.text: 8.1 Layering the customer facing SLA on top

blocks.content: Now say this same team sells the API to external customers with an SLA promising 99.5 percent successful requests, backed by service credits if missed.

sla_target = 0.995                       # 99.5 percent, looser than the SLO
sla_allowed_failures = total_requests * (1 - sla_target)

print(sla_allowed_failures)              # 150000.0

code.content:
sla_target = 0.995                       # 99.5 percent, looser than the SLO
sla_allowed_failures = total_requests * (1 - sla_target)

print(sla_allowed_failures)              # 150000.0

codes.python:
def main():
    total_requests = 30_000_000          # carried over from the SLO calculation above
    sla_target = 0.995                   # 99.5 percent, looser than the SLO
    sla_allowed_failures = total_requests * (1 - sla_target)

    print(sla_allowed_failures)          # 150000.0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: At the SLA level, 150000 failures would still be within contract. But the team never plans to get anywhere near that number, because their internal SLO error budget of 30000 runs out five times sooner. By the time they are anywhere close to breaching the SLA, their own dashboards have already been screaming for weeks.
{"headers":["Level","Target","Allowed failures out of 30 million"],"rows":[["Internal SLO","99.9 percent","30,000"],["External SLA","99.5 percent","150,000"]]}

blocks.title: The SLA number is a customer promise, not a planning target
blocks.content: Never plan capacity or on call response around the SLA number. It exists for contracts and refunds. Plan and alert around the tighter SLO instead.
9. The interview angle

When an interviewer asks how you would think about reliability trade offs for a system, bringing up SLOs and error budgets signals that you think like someone who has actually run a production service, not just designed one on a whiteboard.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396358744-400546308.png
blocks.alt: SLI feeds SLO, which produces an error budget, which drives alerting, and sits stricter than the SLA

blocks.content: ["Explain that reliability and feature velocity are in tension, and an error budget is the tool that makes that tension explicit and manageable","Mention that a full budget is a green light to ship faster, an empty one is a signal to slow down and focus on stability","Bring up burn rate alerting as a more mature answer than a single static threshold","Note the SLO versus SLA distinction if asked about customer commitments, since conflating the two is a common mistake"]
items: Explain that reliability and feature velocity are in tension, and an error budget is the tool that makes that tension explicit and manageable
Mention that a full budget is a green light to ship faster, an empty one is a signal to slow down and focus on stability
Bring up burn rate alerting as a more mature answer than a single static threshold
Note the SLO versus SLA distinction if asked about customer commitments, since conflating the two is a common mistake

blocks.title: A line worth saying out loud in an interview
blocks.text: I would set an internal SLO stricter than whatever SLA we sell externally, track the resulting error budget, and alert on burn rate so the team gets an early warning long before we are anywhere near breaching a customer contract.

blocks.content: That single sentence covers all three terms correctly, shows you understand the gap between them is intentional, and demonstrates you know the practical tool, the error budget, that makes the whole idea actionable rather than theoretical.
